paragraphs.heading: Genes on the sex chromosomes
paragraphs.text: Humans carry 23 pairs of chromosomes. Twenty-two pairs are autosomes, which play no part in deciding sex, and the last pair are the sex chromosomes. Two X chromosomes define a biological female, while one X and one Y define a biological male. The X and Y differ in size and in the genes they hold, and unlike the autosome pairs they are not matching partners. Sex linkage is the name for the way a trait, and how it shows up, follows sex when the gene version behind it, called an allele, sits on one of these sex chromosomes.

paragraphs.heading: Why the X matters more
paragraphs.text: The X chromosome holds an estimated 1400 genes, most of them tied to tissue development and to human disorders. The Y carries the SRY gene, which helps build several male sex characteristics, plus roughly 200 other genes, many of whose known jobs are linked to disease. Since the X is bigger and holds several times as many genes, X-linked conditions far outnumber Y-linked ones.

paragraphs.heading: Three patterns in humans
paragraphs.text: In humans, sex-linked traits follow three patterns: X-linked recessive, X-linked dominant and Y-linked. In all three, what happens depends on the sex of the parent and on the sex of the child. That sets them apart from ordinary dominant and recessive traits carried on autosomes. Classical genetics tests whether an animal's trait is sex-linked with a mating experiment known as a reciprocal cross.

paragraphs.heading: X-linked recessive
paragraphs.text: In X-linked recessive inheritance, a female (XX) shows the trait only with two copies of the allele, while a male (XY) needs just one. So these conditions turn up in males far more often. A female with a single copy is called a carrier, and only females can be carriers, since a male has no second X with a working copy of the gene. Fathers hand only a Y to their sons, so an affected son must get the allele from his mother. A son of a healthy carrier has a 50% chance of being affected, and every daughter of an affected father and a non-carrier mother will be a carrier.

paragraphs.heading: X-linked dominant
paragraphs.text: In X-linked dominant inheritance, a single copy of the allele is enough to cause the trait. Here females are affected more often than males, because they have two X chromosomes. When the mother is affected and the father is not, each child, son or daughter, has a 50% chance of being affected. When the father is affected and the mother is not, every daughter is affected and no son is, because daughters receive his X and sons his Y. A few of these conditions, such as Aicardi syndrome, kill males before birth or as newborns, so they seem to strike only females.

paragraphs.heading: Carriers who show the trait
paragraphs.text: A carrier female usually does not show the trait. In rare cases, though, the normal switching off of half her X chromosomes is skewed, so it mostly silences the X chromosomes from one parent. The X chromosomes from the other parent are then expressed out of proportion, and the trait can show to varying degrees. Because effects like this make X-linked traits so variable in females, some scholars now suggest dropping the words dominant and recessive for X-linked inheritance.

paragraphs.heading: Y-linked and other systems
paragraphs.text: A Y-linked condition passes only from father to son and shows up in every generation. Animals that settle sex in other ways follow other rules. Birds use the ZW system, which flips the mammal pattern: males are ZZ and females are ZW. In humans and other mammals genes decide sex, but not in every organism; in some reptiles the environment decides, and in some worms it depends on where they are.
